blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Reward models score responses for preference optimization, filtering and ranking, and pooling scores across prompts needs them to be comparable. Yet pairwise evaluation compares two responses to the same prompt, so any score component shared by a prompt's responses cancels and goes untested. We study this component by comparing between-prompt variation in model scores with the same variation in human ratings of the same responses. We propose a human-referenced audit, built from a between-prompt variance share, a sibling-rating regression and prompt substitutions, and apply it to eighteen released scorers and six matched training conditions. We find that scores cluster by prompt more than the ratings do: on HelpSteer2, six reward models have between-prompt shares of 0.34 to 0.64 against a human share near zero. Replacing the original prompt with a fixed instruction keeps substantial clustering but weakens agreement with prompt-level human ratings, so clustering alone does not show agreement with humans. Part of that variation is useful: subtracting prompt means lowers the helpfulness of globally selected responses, and scores stay sensitive to a wrong prompt even when training shuffles prompt means. We propose that reward evaluation check between-prompt variation, sensitivity to a wrong prompt and usefulness for selection separately.
blocks.zh: 奖励模式对优惠优化、过滤和排位的评分答复,将评分汇集到各提示之间,需要它们具有可比性。 然而双向评价将两个回复比作同一个即时,所以一个即时回复共享的任何分数部分都会取消,未经测试. 我们通过比较模型分数的瞬间变化和相同反应的人类分数的相同变化来研究这个组成部分. 我们建议进行一次人参考审计,根据瞬间差异份额、兄弟级回归和即时替换情况进行,并将它适用于18个解聘的计分员和6个相应的培训条件。 我们发现比收视率更迅速的分数组:在HelpSteer2上,6个奖励模式的瞬间股权为0.34到0.64,而人类股权接近0。 用固定指令取代原始的提示保持实质性的集群化,但削弱与即时级人类评级的一致,因此单是集群化并不能显示与人类的一致. 其中一部分变化是有用的:减去即时反应意味着降低全球所选反应的有用性,分数对错误的即时反应保持敏感,即使培训即时反应。 我们建议,奖励评估在瞬间的变化、对错误的迅速性和单独选择的有用性之间进行检查。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en: Reward models assign scores that steer preference optimization, data selection and model rankings ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . They are trained on pairwise preferences between two responses to one prompt ( Liu et al., 2024a ) or on ratings of single responses ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024a ) , and validated on pairwise benchmarks such as RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; Malik et al., 2026 ) , where a model is correct when it ranks the two responses to a prompt in the order humans preferred.

blocks.en:
A pairwise check cannot detect a score component that is shared by every response to a prompt, because that
component cancels when the two scores are compared. We call it the per-prompt term. Under the Bradley–Terry
objective the loss depends only on differences of rewards within a prompt, so the term is unconstrained and the
reward is identified only up to a function of the prompt ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Hasanaliyev et al., 2026 ; Lamparth et al., 2026 ) . The term leaves within-prompt uses
unchanged, such as best-of- n n selection and policy optimization with a per-prompt baseline ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) . It can change decisions that pool scores across prompts, such as a
global reward threshold that filters training data ( Yu et al., 2025 ) and a mean reward over different prompt
sets. The practical question is whether these differences reflect useful quality variation, arbitrary offsets, or
both. Prior work has found weak prompt sensitivity in pairwise reward gaps and prompt-level offsets that can be
estimated and subtracted ( Mao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . We test how
between-prompt score variation compares with human ratings of the same responses and whether removing it improves
global selection, across reward models and generative judges.

blocks.en:
We propose a human-referenced audit along three dimensions: variation between prompts, agreement with human
ratings, and sensitivity to prompt–response mismatch, that is, to a wrong prompt. The between-prompt variance
share of a score, an intraclass correlation, is compared with the same share in the human ratings. A sibling-rating
regression regresses a score on the rating of the shown response and on the rating of a sibling response to the
same prompt, and controlled prompt substitutions test the sensitivity. We apply the audit to eighteen
released scorers on up to three rating sets and to six training conditions at two sizes of one base-model family.
To our knowledge, this is the first comparison of language reward models’ between-prompt variance shares with
human ratings of the same responses across rating sets with different rating protocols. For
the six core models, the 7B to 8B reward models scored under every condition, substantial clustering remains when
one fixed instruction replaces the prompt, with changed prompt means, while agreement with human prompt-level
ratings weakens on HelpSteer (Figure 1 ). Yet subtracting prompt means lowers helpfulness in a
global-selection task on HelpSteer, including when the means come from independent reference responses. Matched
training further shows that a large mismatch penalty does not require correct prompt-mean supervision: the mean
penalty differs by about 0.3 score standard deviations or less between the shuffled-mean and the true-mean arms.

blocks.en:
The per-prompt term of a score is the component shared by the scores of the responses to the same prompt. Prompt mean
scores are averages over the responses a rating set samples, so every prompt-level quantity is relative to that
response set. The between-prompt variance share, or share for
short, is the proportion of the total score variance that lies between prompts on a stated set of responses. The
human prompt mean is the average rating of the responses to a prompt, and the human reference is the same share
computed from the ratings of the same responses. A larger model share need not indicate an erroneous offset,
because it can also arise when the model compresses the differences within a prompt.

blocks.en: 3.2 Prompt substitutions
blocks.zh: 3.2 即时替换

blocks.en:
Each response is scored under several prompt conditions, and each condition is compared with the original-prompt
condition (Table 3 in the appendix). In the generic-prompt condition (response-only for
short) every response is scored under one fixed generic instruction instead of its own prompt ("Please
respond."), and the share is computed again over the original prompt grouping. This measures clustering by the
original prompt when the scorer receives only the response and a fixed instruction. In the
prompt-only condition every prompt is scored with one fixed generic reply, and that reward is correlated across
prompts with the prompts’ mean reward under the original prompt. In the transplants
every response is scored under its own prompt and under wrong prompts: four random prompts, the four nearest by
word overlap or by embedding, four length-matched prompts, or three related tasks written by an instruction model ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . The match margin is the response’s reward under its own prompt minus its mean reward under
the wrong ones, in units of the standard deviation of the original-condition rewards, and the match accuracy is the
share of responses whose own prompt scores above every wrong prompt. In the paraphrase condition every response is
scored under three rewordings of its own prompt, and we report the mean absolute shift in reward and the mean signed shift.

blocks.en:
Prompt-centered pooling subtracts from a response’s score the mean score of other responses to the same prompt
before scores are compared across prompts. With a fixed group size, leave-one-out centering preserves every
within-prompt ranking and rescales the within-prompt differences by k / ( k − 1 ) k/(k-1) . We measure the pooled Spearman correlation of the raw and of the centered score
with the raw and with the prompt-centered human rating, and the mean rating of the 30% highest-scored responses.
A centered score also carries the sampling noise of its baseline, so we center on one, two or three siblings and
on an independent pool of twelve generated responses per prompt.

To test the training signal we compare six training conditions within the Qwen3 family at 0.6B and 1.7B, all on
the same 6,667 HelpSteer2 training preference pairs. The two main arms fit a regression head on the helpfulness
ratings and the Bradley–Terry loss on the released preference labels, tuned with equal search budgets and the
same held-out selection criterion (Appendix B ), with five seeds per chosen configuration. The arms
differ in the loss and in its supervision: the helpfulness ratings or the released pairwise preference labels.
Four control arms separate the two. A regression on the within-prompt rating gap alone sees no absolute level, the
full pointwise loss with each prompt’s mean rating shuffled across prompts sees a wrong level, a Bradley–Terry
loss on the rating margin sees the size of the gap. A regression on binarized ratings sees only which response
was preferred.

blocks.en:
We use the validation split of HelpSteer2 (519 prompts, 511 distinct first user turns, 1,038 responses) for every
model, and its training split for the models whose documentation states no training on HelpSteer2, because
several open reward models were trained on that split. Multi-turn prompts, about 31% of the set, carry earlier assistant turns, so every share is also reported on the 356 single-turn prompts. The second rating set is HelpSteer’s validation split, 378 single-turn prompts with
four rated responses each. The third is 1,000 Reddit posts of the Stanford Human Preferences validation split with
four voted comments each.

attribute model of DPA), for which the reward is the helpfulness head. ArmoRM and DPA were trained on HelpSteer’s
ratings as their documentation states, so their HelpSteer rows come with a documented training-data exposure that has no row-level confirmation. For breadth we add two size ladders of the Skywork-Reward-V2

expected helpfulness digit from 1 to 5, Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B-Reward, which shares the 70B judge’s base, and Qwen2.5-CascadeRL-RM-72B, released in 2026. blocks.en: 5 Human references differ across rating sets

blocks.en:
We use the ratings’ between-prompt share as a rating-set-specific human reference. A larger model share means
that a larger fraction of the model’s score variance lies between prompts, and it does not by itself establish an
incorrect prompt offset. On HelpSteer, where four responses sampled from one model were rated independently, helpfulness has a share of
0.26 [0.20, 0.33] on the 378 validation prompts the models are scored on. On HelpSteer2 the prompt explains almost
none of the helpfulness ratings. Its annotators rated the two responses to a prompt in sequence, and the two
ratings are weakly negatively correlated, with a leave-one-out correlation of − 0.08 -0.08 (Table 7 ). The share
is − 0.01 -0.01 [ − 0.11 -0.11 , 0.10] on the validation split the models are scored on and within 0.07 of zero on the
training split and on single-turn prompts. The two sets differ in response source and in rating protocol. We cannot
separate these influences, so we report the two references separately. Under an independent additive-noise model rater noise attenuates the observed share, and dividing by a reliability borrowed from HelpSteer2’s raters puts HelpSteer’s value between 0.32 and 0.55 (Appendix C ). We use that range as a sensitivity analysis rather than as a ceiling, because the noise model is an assumption and a scorer that compresses within-prompt differences has a higher share than the quality it predicts. The Reddit vote share is context only, because votes carry exposure
(Appendix C ).

blocks.en: 10 Related work
blocks.zh: 10 相关工作

blocks.en:
Reward models and judges respond to length ( Singhal et al., 2024 ) , style and formatting ( Liu et al., 2024b ) ,
and superficial markers of quality ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Wang et al. (2025) show that a Bradley–Terry
reward model learns a prompt-template offset, predict each prompt’s mean reward from a head on the prompt, and
subtract it before policy optimization. Our global-selection tests show that subtracting prompt means can remove variation associated with
independently rated quality. Landesberg (2026) decomposes judge and reference scores into between-prompt and within-prompt variation and studies the consequences for best-of- n n selection. Sun et al. (2025) compare objectives across annotation designs. Hasanaliyev et al. (2026) predict per-prompt mean rewards from a prompt embedding on held-out prompts,
with 32 responses per prompt and without human-rating references, and report about half of the variance explained for three pairwise-trained models. Our probe uses two responses per prompt and human references, a different setting (Appendix C ). Prior work tests prompt substitution through changes in reward gaps ( Mao et al., 2025 ) , augments
training with cross-prompt response combinations ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , and evaluates the preference for on-topic
over off-topic answers ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . These pairwise contrasts detect response-specific
mismatch and cancel shifts shared by both responses. We complement them with fixed-response contrasts across
prompts and with human-referenced between-prompt variation, including pointwise models and judges. Group-relative baselines in policy optimization ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) remove the per-prompt term from the gradient, margin-based pair
selection ( Deng et al., 2025 ) cancels it by construction, and prompt filtering by pooled raw rewards ( Yu et al., 2025 ) uses it. The sibling-rating regression and the prompt-only condition are adapted from probes for
audio-language judges of generated music ( Modrzejewski and Radzikowski, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en: 11 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 11 结论

blocks.en:
We find that pairwise accuracy leaves score comparisons across prompts untested. On both HelpSteer sets, released
scorers have larger between-prompt variance shares than the observed human ratings. For the six core models,
replacing the original prompt with a fixed generic prompt preserves substantial clustering while weakening
agreement with prompt-level human ratings on HelpSteer, so the amount of clustering does not establish
agreement with human judgments. Some prompt-level variation is useful: full centering lowers helpfulness in our
global-selection task, including with independent reference responses. Matched training also shows that large
mismatch penalties need no correct prompt-mean supervision. We propose that reward evaluation distinguish
between-prompt variation, mismatch sensitivity, and usefulness for selection. Centering for global
selection should be validated against the intended quality criterion.

blocks.en: Ethical considerations

blocks.en:
The study uses released datasets under their terms (HelpSteer2 and HelpSteer under CC-BY-4.0, RewardBench and its
second version under ODC-By, the Stanford Human Preferences set under the terms its card states for Reddit
content, used for research only and not redistributed) and open model weights under their licences, without new
human annotation. We plan to release the scoring and analysis code, the scores and source identifiers of every scored response,
and the generated paraphrase and related-task prompt sets, subject to the source datasets’ redistribution terms.
Global filtering can change which prompt groups are represented in the selected data even when within-prompt
rankings remain unchanged, so applications should assess those changes against the intended quality criterion.

HelpSteer’s validation release has 503 prompts with one to four rated responses. Every HelpSteer analysis keeps the 378 with exactly four, and the 125 others are left out rather than imputed. Of the 519 HelpSteer2 validation prompts, 511 first turns are distinct as written and 509 after lower-casing and whitespace normalization, and grouped folds and held-out splits use the 509. HelpSteer2’s training split has 10,161 prompts, of which the 10,160 with two responses enter the share. Multi-turn prompts are passed as their turns with the rated response as the last assistant turn, through each model’s chat template. The DPA model uses its fixed string template. Inputs are truncated at 4,096 tokens on the
right. The generic reply of the prompt-only condition is "Thank you for your question. I will do my best to
help.", and the fixed instructions of the generic-prompt condition are "Please respond.", "Write something." and the
empty prompt. The random transplant draws four other prompts per response with a fixed seed. The nearest
transplants take the four prompts with the highest TF-IDF cosine over words or the highest cosine between
sentence embeddings (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5), excluding prompts from the same conversation. The length-matched
transplant draws four random prompts within 10% of the original prompt’s word count. The paraphrases and related-task
prompts were written by Qwen3-8B (sampling at temperature 0.7 with a fixed seed) from two fixed instructions. A
variant that repeated the original or was shorter than five words was rejected and regenerated once, after which
50 of the 519 prompts (9.6%) had no valid paraphrase and were dropped from that condition, and every prompt had
three related tasks. The response probes are ridge, kernel ridge, boosted trees and a multilayer perceptron on two
sentence embeddings (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 and bge-large-en-v1.5) with text features and a topic cluster,
cross-validated by prompt. The judges were asked for a helpfulness rating from 1 to 5 and scored as the expected
value over the digit tokens. On the validation responses no judge puts under 0.9 of the mass on the digits, and the lowest digit mass is 1.00, 0.99 and 0.94 for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. On HelpSteer the share of rows under 0.9 is 0.2%, 8.2% and 2.3% on the real rows and 0.3%, 23.9% and 5.9% on transplanted rows, and under the empty reply, a condition not reported for the judges, the 70B judge has 0.87 of its rows under 0.9. The top digit is 5
for 0.55, 0.77 and 0.69 of the validation responses and the median expected value is 4.62, 4.83 and 4.89.

The two main matched arms were tuned with 24 trials per arm (tree-structured Parzen estimator, median pruner) over the
learning rate (log-uniform from 10 − 6 10^{-6} to 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} ), batch size (8, 16, 32), warm-up ratio (0 to 0.1),
schedule (constant, cosine), weight decay (0, 0.01, 0.1) and epochs (1, 2), on within-prompt accuracy over held-out
training pairs grouped by first user turn. The chosen configurations were, for the regression arm, learning rate 1.1 × 10 − 6 1.1\times 10^{-6} , batch 8, warm-up 0.098, constant schedule, no weight decay, two epochs (held-out accuracy
0.718), and for the Bradley–Terry arm, learning rate 5.3 × 10 − 6 5.3\times 10^{-6} , batch 16, warm-up 0.054, cosine
schedule, weight decay 0.01, one epoch (0.744). The gap-only arm fits ( d r − d h ) 2 / 4 (d_{r}-d_{h})^{2}/4 for the two responses of
a pair, with d r d_{r} the difference of their rewards and d h d_{h} the difference of their ratings, and the shuffled-mean
arm fits the full pointwise loss after the mean rating of each pair has been permuted across pairs. Both use the
regression arm’s configuration. The pairs are HelpSteer2’s released training preferences: 8,677 pairs, less 1,911 ties and 99 pairs whose first turn opens a validation conversation, leave 6,667 pairs over 6,089 conversations. The chosen response is given by the sign of the preference strength, and it is rated higher on helpfulness in 5,494 pairs, equal in 1,052 and lower in 121. Each arm is the base with a bias-free linear head on the final state of the last non-padding token, with every parameter trained, fp32 master weights and bf16 autocast. The regression arms fit squared error to the standardized rating of each of the 13,334 responses, the Bradley–Terry arm fits − log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( r c − r r ) -\log\sigma(r_{c}-r_{r}) for the chosen and rejected rewards, the rating-margin arm subtracts the helpfulness gap in raw points inside the sigmoid (zero for 1,173 pairs), and the binarized arm regresses on 1 for the chosen and 0 for the rejected response. A tied score counts as wrong in every accuracy. The search holds out whole conversations until at least 10% of the pairs are held out (6,000 fit and 667 held-out pairs over 609 conversations), and the final arms retrain on all 6,667 pairs with seeds 0 to 4. Training inputs were truncated at 2,048 tokens, which affected 13 of the 13,334 training sequences (8 pairs). Scoring ran in bf16 on RTX 4090 cards and training on 96 GB cards with torch 2.14.0, transformers 5.17.0
and optuna 4.5.0.

The five policies are Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B (the anchor), Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
as released, decoding greedily with at most 2,048 new tokens on the 356 single-turn validation prompts. The four
prompt mixes are the prompts above and at or below the median word count, and the two halves of a twenty-cluster
TF-IDF k-means over the first turns. Each of the twenty assignments gives every policy one mix drawn uniformly, and
an assignment that puts all five on the same mix is redrawn. The judge sees the prompt and the two responses labelled
A and B, is asked "Which response is more helpful to the user? Answer with the letter A or B only.", and its answer is the probability of A renormalized over the two letters, averaged over both orders. The filtering policies were trained with DPO ( β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 , two epochs, 32 pairs per step, 2,449 pairs per arm), as a full fine-tune judged by the 70B judge and as a low-rank variant (rank 16) judged by the 24B judge, with the learning rate chosen in each case on the random arm’s held-out conversations.

blocks.en: Table 15: HelpSteer2 validation agreement and top-30% selection under raw and sibling-centered scores.
